newsitem.title: FRANCE: Early vote hinders French Socialists - pollster.
newsitem.headline: Early vote hinders French Socialists - pollster.

text.p: The short French election campaign will hinder the opposition Socialists but if the vote comes down to a simple decision between Left or Right they stand a fighting chance, Edouard Lecerf of the Louis Harris polling institute told Reuters Financial Television on Thursday.
While French financial markets are hanging on the outcome of every poll, Lecerf warned that opinion polls would probably be very volatile given that there is only a month left to the vote.
French President Jacques Chirac called a snap parliamentary election for May 25/June 1 on Monday.

Asked whether the Socialist Party could make up ground on the ruling centre-right coalition Lecerf said, "Yes...If (the decision) is to vote for (the) Left or Right, France is always roughly 50/50. That may allow the left wing to recover many many more votes from the level it has now."
One factor that may disadvantage the Socialists in this very short campaign is that it will be fielding many new candidates, Lecerf said in the interview.

The first opinion poll since the election was called, released late on Tuesday by CSA Institute, showed the centre-right would win 322 of the National Assembly's 577 seats to 201 for the Socialists and 20 for the Communists.
Lecerf said it was unclear what the main issues would be in the campaign and the large number of voters who have yet to make a decision meant the picture could change very quickly.

"A few days ago everyone thought that Europe would be the main topic...Right now it's not so clear. President Chirac talked about Europe of course, but he also talked about right wing and left wing positions, he talked about the extreme right, and the values he wanted to point out."
"So we don't know exactly what people are going to do. Are they going to vote Left or Right? For or against Europe? For men or for women?" he said.
He cautioned against reading too much into opinion polls measuring individual politicians' popularity, especially Chirac or Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
The vote "will in a way be partly anti or for Chirac," he said. "Popularity is not the vote, that's true all the time, but unpopularity is not the vote either."

He said it was usual for around 30 percent of voters to be undecided at this stage of the campaign. He said it could drop quickly but evidence from the 1995 presidential election showed many voters decided how they would vote at the last minute.
Because of that, Lecerf said there was always a chance that even the last polls might accurately predict the ultimate outcome and an undecided five percent could still swing the result.
"The problem is that the electorate is very volatile...and five percent is a majority."
